On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the one forcing his way out while Sitaram is the guard at the locked door: Udayaditya draws his sword, orders Sitaram to open the door, and overpowers the situation, while Sitaram—refusing to raise arms against the prince who saved his life twice—disarms himself and asks to be bound so he will be spared punishment.

On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the relationship is inverted: Sitaram is now the one who throws open the prison door, takes command, and tells the prince to come out because the prison is on fire. Udayaditya, long confined, emerges dazed and helpless, asking "What should I do? Where should I go?" and Sitaram answers "Come, come with me"—so the former guard now leads and directs, and the former prince passively follows.

He first ordered two Pathan men to murder Basanta Ray on the road as he traveled to Jessore (at the Simultali inn), but they balked and did not kill him. Basanta Ray is finally ended by a direct execution order signed by Pratapaditya and carried out by Muktiyar Khan’s forces: Abdul beheads the praying old king with a sword.
In the women’s inner quarters/Mahishi’s room disguised as a middle-aged woman, and in the king’s palace chamber as Ramai Bhand the court jester.
Mangala/Rukmini’s poisoned “medicine,” secretly obtained through Matangini for the Rajmahishi, killed Surma on the eve of exile.
Ramchandra Ray takes another wife, so Vibha finally arrives only to find her husband has married someone else and her royal home is closed to her.

Rukmini extracts Udayaditya’s signet ring from him, and Bhagavat uses its seal to stamp a forged petition making it look like Udayaditya is accusing Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor. Bhagavat then presents this “intercepted” petition to Pratapaditya as proof of Udayaditya’s plotting, giving Pratapaditya the pretext to imprison him.

After Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Pratapaditya began watching Udayaditya closely. So when Udayaditya kept aiding the dismissed Sitaram and Bhagavat—and Surma secretly continued those payments through her maid, later leaked via Mangala—the news reached Pratapaditya, and he answered by ordering Surma sent to her paternal home.

It expresses his emptiness and orphaned grief: those he loved once called him no longer answer, so his song has no joy or audience. He gives it once as a soft, almost private lament at the Raigarh sunset while insisting he is content, and again as open heartbreak with Vibha before Surma’s silent, empty room after the family’s ruin is confirmed.

Her failed attack lets Udayaditya reach Raigarh; crazed by that defeat, she returns alive, names Sitaram, Basanta Ray, and Udayaditya as conspirators, guides Muktiyar Khan’s troops to Raigarh, and gets the Yubaraj seized—so Pratapaditya’s death order for Basanta Ray is carried out.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra with deliberate coolness—minimal ceremony, few retainers, and an audience dominated by routine state business—so that Ramchandra is made to feel small rather than welcomed as royalty. Ramchandra later answers by turning Pratapaditya’s standing into a court joke: his ministers and jester daily halve Pratapaditya’s dignity, tracing his line from an earthworm and a blood-sucking leech and claiming his house owes its kingship to Ramchandra’s own grandfather, while Ramchandra laughs and lets the assault on his father-in-law’s rank pass or encourages it. Pratapaditya asserts superiority by withholding honor; Ramchandra asserts superiority by explicitly stripping Pratapaditya of it.

By living as the outskirts widow Mangala, befriending palace servants, and using the queen mother’s secret attempt to drug Surma’s “medicine” as poison prepared with tantric rites, leading to Surma’s fatal poisoning.

His wish “not to be the sole heir” becomes the truth he finally acts on: branded unfit and ruined, he begs Pratapaditya to release him, swears before Ma-Kali never to claim Jessore’s kingdom, throne, or scepter, and departs for Kashi.

Nayanchand, afraid to hand it to Pratapaditya, diverts the letter to the Mahishi, who lets Basanta Ray see it; they then conceal its real threat—that Ramchandra had renounced Vibha—and announce instead that he had written asking for her to be sent to Chandradwip, making Vibha believe he still understood and trusted her.

He blocks the palace canal with large salwood logs, but Rammohan and his men haul the boat up and over them; meanwhile the guards’ stones miss, no flintlock/gunpowder is ready, and the chase boat arrives too late.

The sitar becomes a mirror of his loss: once his constant joyful companion, he leaves it behind, vows not to play it again, and later finds its strings broken and untunable. Its silence reflects his own emptiness as Udayaditya is imprisoned and the people he loved and sang for are gone.

Earlier, Udayaditya was bold and ready to confront danger to protect oppressed subjects; after Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitant and passive, so he no longer intervenes or gives the help he once would.
He rescues Udayaditya from the prison caused by their forged petition and helps him escape the burning palace.
He carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down the improvised rope from the palace roof into their boat, and later lifts/carries the fainted Vibha out of the hostile palace and sets her into a palanquin.

She shifts from being heavily overdressed as a royal bride—thick gold bangles, a huge diamond bracelet, a large nose ring, and elaborately styled hair—to presenting herself as an ordinary veiled woman or beggar, entering the palace like a maidservant rather than a queen.

In his bedchamber, the window is a haunted memorial space: Udayaditya leaves Surma’s seat empty, watches the unchanged moonlight, garden, and breeze, and keeps listening for her voice, so it symbolizes loss, longing, and an impossible return. In prison, the same kind of window becomes a source of freedom: through its small opening he sees sky, birds, bamboo, and a temple, and watching birds fly makes him believe his cage will break. The window’s few feet of light become the one place he feels naturally free, while darkness and the bed turn into his true prison.

It starts as Sitaram’s performance of charm: singing endearments like “Pranpriye” to borrow from Rukmini/Mangala, who answers with affectionate possession rather than open usury. The debt goes unpaid, Sitaram evades repayment through the “my mother took my money” excuse, and their meetings turn into secret conspiracy for Udayaditya. When Sitaram visits after Udayaditya’s imprisonment and threatens to burn her house, ruin her, and drive her away, Rukmini’s wounded pride hardens into ownership: “he is *my* Yubaraj.” Later, after the prison fire, Sitaram slips back to rob her, expecting her dead, and finds her half-drowned, trembling, and full of razed hope. His reflexive pet names enrage her; she searches for a curved blade, promises to put Sitaram and Udayaditya in the oven/pyre before Yama is satisfied, and he flees. From then on she turns their old intimacy into denunciation, telling Pratapaditya the truth and offering to help trap them.

Sitaram first lets the guardhouse fire pull every watchman away so Udayaditya can be taken out, then relies on loyal men to sabotage the firefighting—useless water-pouring, broken pots, confusion—so the blaze burns on. It becomes a cover-up when his men burn Udayaditya’s now-empty cell, fill it with bones, a skull, and the sword, and stage screams plus a roof collapse to announce the prince’s “death.” He then supports the story by taking back and destroying incriminating letters, planting the melted sword as proof, spreading the rumor in court, and fleeing Jessore once Mangala’s knowledge of the escape makes him unsafe.
He shows no gratitude, mocks Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son, and assumes the rescue was done mainly for Vibha’s sake rather than from loyalty to him.

He weaponizes Delhi itself: Sitaram and Bhagavat fabricate a petition stamped with Prince Udayaditya’s seal, supposedly sent by the prince to the Emperor accusing Pratapaditya of treason. Bhagavat delivers it to the king as proof of his son’s treachery, turning the once-ridiculed threat of the Emperor’s anger into “evidence” that lets him imprison Udayaditya.

Braiding Vibha’s hair had been Surma’s intimate, daily act of care and recognition; after Surma’s death it becomes the ritual whose non-performance marks her absence. Vibha sits waiting as if Surma will come, but no one comes, so her hair stays undone—an outward sign of neglect, grief, and the empty place Surma left in the palace.
